title: Low & Predictable Latency
summary: Getting alarms, voice and video through on time, every time, not just on average.

opener.promise: Alarms and calls on time, not just on average
opener.problem: Now and then an alarm waits behind a large download before reaching the nurses’ station.

beats.heading: The alarm stuck behind a download

caption.headline: The alarm stuck behind a download
caption.takeaway: For alarms, voice and remote procedures, the rare slow message matters more than the typical one.

beats.body:
A bedside monitor raises an alarm. Its message is tiny, but the channel is busy: a workstation is pulling a large image and dozens of devices are taking turns.

Most of the time the alarm gets through almost instantly. Occasionally it waits much longer — and the same happens to voice calls and to the video in a remotely supported procedure.
beats.bottomLine: For alarms, voice and remote procedures, the rare slow message matters more than the typical one.
beats.sceneDescription: A road runs from a bedside monitor to the nurses’ station. Each alarm is an ambulance; a large download is a line of grey lorries on the same single lane. Most ambulances drive straight through, but now and then one gets stuck behind a lorry. Each arrival adds a block to an arrivals board behind the road, and the late ones are red.

callout.title: Why alarms sometimes wait
points: Alarms share the channel with large downloads
Usually the road is clear and the alarm is instant
Now and then it is stuck behind a download

beats.heading: Fast on average is not enough

caption.headline: Fast on average is not enough
caption.takeaway: [[latency|Latency]] has a long tail; Wi-Fi 7 explicitly targets the worst-case delays{{be-latency-objective}}.
caption.technical: 802.11be’s scope includes improved worst-case latency and [[jitter|jitter]]{{be-latency-objective}}; [[tail-latency|tail latency]] is the slowest messages’ delay.

beats.body:
[[latency|Latency]] is how long a message takes to arrive. Two things matter: the typical delay, and how much it varies — [[jitter]] and [[tail-latency|tail latency]], the delay of the slowest messages.

Wi-Fi 7 was designed with this in mind: the scope of IEEE 802.11be includes improved worst-case latency and jitter {{be-latency-objective}}.
beats.bottomLine: Wi-Fi 7 is the first generation that explicitly targets the worst-case delays that make real-time clinical communication unreliable.
beats.sceneDescription: The camera moves to the arrivals board. A tall green column on the left shows most alarms arriving on time; a thin trail of red blocks stretches to the right, showing the few that arrived very late: the tail. The board is labelled illustrative.

questions.q: How much lower is Wi-Fi 7 latency?
questions.a: There is no single figure: worst-case delay depends on load, device mix and configuration. The standard targets improved worst-case latency and jitter{{be-latency-objective}}; measure it in a pilot with your own alarm and voice systems.

callout.title: The average hides the tail
points: A few arrive very late, and those are the ones that matter
Wi-Fi 7 was designed to cut the worst-case delays{{be-latency-objective}}

beats.heading: Three ways to avoid waiting

caption.headline: Three ways to avoid waiting
caption.takeaway: Multi-link, protected [[twt|TWT]] slots and [[multi-ru|Multi-RU]] each remove a different reason urgent messages wait{{rtwt-be}}.
caption.technical: [[mlo|MLO]] uses whichever link wins access first{{mlo-tid-mapping}}; restricted service periods clear the air{{rtwt-protect}}.

beats.body:
Wi-Fi 7 combines three features to cut the long waits:

**[[mlo|Multi-link operation]]** sends the alarm on whichever band is free {{mlo-bands}}. **[[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]]**, a form of [[twt|Target Wake Time]], reserves protected time for latency-sensitive traffic {{rtwt-protect}}. **[[multi-ru|Multi-RU]]** fits urgent traffic into spare parts of the channel {{multi-ru-be}}.
beats.bottomLine: These features work together to remove the specific situations that make urgent messages wait.
beats.deepDive: MLO lets traffic move to the link that gains channel access first, with TID-to-link mapping steering traffic classes {{mlo-tid-mapping}}. Restricted TWT service periods require supporting stations to end transmissions before the period starts {{rtwt-protect}}. Multi-RU allows flexible RU combinations per station {{multi-ru-be}}. Each one addresses a different cause of queuing delay.
beats.sceneDescription: Wi-Fi 7’s road has two lanes, standing for two bands. An ambulance takes whichever lane has no download ahead. At regular protected slots the lorries pull over onto the shoulder and stop, so any ambulance passes straight through. The new arrivals board fills with green blocks on the left and almost no red.

questions.a: It depends on the cause. MLO helps when one band is congested{{mlo-tid-mapping}}, Restricted TWT when long transmissions block urgent traffic{{rtwt-protect}}, and Multi-RU when the channel has spare fragments{{multi-ru-be}}.

callout.title: Three ways to avoid waiting
points: [[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]]: downloads pause in protected slots{{rtwt-protect}}
[[multi-ru|Multi-RU]]: urgent traffic fits into spare room{{multi-ru-be}}

beats.heading: A shorter tail, not just a faster average

caption.headline: A shorter tail, not just a faster average
caption.takeaway: The goal is predictability: urgent traffic arriving on time, consistently{{latency-histogram-illustrative}}.
caption.technical: Results vary with load, device mix and configuration; pilot latency-sensitive applications before rollout{{be-latency-objective}}.

beats.body:
Earlier generations improved typical speed but left the slow tail: a busy band, a long transmission or a crowded channel could still hold up a message. Wi-Fi 7 targets that tail directly {{be-latency-objective}}.

The charts here show the shape of the change, not measured values {{latency-histogram-illustrative}}.
beats.bottomLine: The goal is predictability: urgent traffic arriving on time consistently, which is what clinical workflows depend on.
beats.deepDive: Worst-case latency depends on deployment: channel load, device mix, client support for MLO and restricted TWT, and configuration of traffic classes. No figures are shown here because results vary by environment; evaluate latency-sensitive applications in a pilot before rollout {{latency-histogram-illustrative}}.
beats.sceneDescription: Two roads, one above the other, with the same alarms and downloads. Above, the earlier generation: one lane, and its arrivals board has a trail of red late arrivals. Below, Wi-Fi 7: two lanes and protected slots, and its board is bunched on the left with almost no tail. Both boards are labelled illustrative.

callout.title: A shorter tail
points: Earlier Wi-Fi: fast on average, with some late alarms
Results vary with load and devices, so pilot first

beats.heading: Alarms and calls that arrive on time

caption.headline: Alarms and calls that arrive on time
caption.takeaway: Include worst-case latency in Wi-Fi 7 acceptance tests for alarm, voice and video.

beats.body:
Clinical alarms, nurse calls, voice and remotely supported procedures need consistent delivery, not just a good average. Wi-Fi 7's latency features support that consistency on busy networks.

Wireless networks remain one part of the alarm chain, so clinical alarm systems should still follow their manufacturers' validated configurations.
beats.bottomLine: Include worst-case latency in Wi-Fi 7 acceptance testing for alarm, voice and video applications, not only average throughput.
beats.sceneDescription: The Wi-Fi 7 road at a busy moment: downloads keep flowing, ambulances keep arriving on time, and the arrivals board stays bunched on the left. The board is labelled illustrative.

questions.q: Can we rely on Wi-Fi 7 for clinical alarms?
questions.a: Wi-Fi is one link in the alarm chain. Wi-Fi 7 improves consistency, but alarm systems should still follow their manufacturers’ validated configurations and your clinical engineering testing.

callout.title: What to test
points: Worst-case delay for alarms, voice and video, not just averages
Busy-hour tests with real downloads running
Alarm systems in their manufacturers’ validated configurations
